name: Clay mask for pores

lead: A clay mask is a paste of mineral clay applied to the face and rinsed off once dry. People use it to take shine off oily skin and to make pores look smaller and skin look matte.

Clays such as bentonite are described as absorbent materials, with the calcium form adsorbing fats and oils, and kaolin is listed as an ingredient in facial masks. Clay particles have a large surface area and soak up surface oil as the mask dries. No clinical trial of clay masks for pore appearance was identified.

paras: Users apply a layer to clean skin, leave it for about the time it takes to dry, rinse it off, and repeat once or twice a week. It is often applied only to the oily T-zone.
Kaolin is described as generally safe with possible mild irritation, and trace crystalline silica may occur in some products. An FDA consumer warning on one bentonite product has been referenced.

chain: Less shine and oil in pores
angle.text: Clay masks with kaolin or bentonite absorb surface oil, which takes down shine and makes pores look smaller and skin more matte. The oil-absorbing action is described in reference sources, and the effect on pore size has not been tested in trials.

lead: A clay mask is a skin-care product containing mineral clays such as kaolin or bentonite, applied as a paste to the face and rinsed off after drying. Marketing and community discussion commonly present it as a way to absorb surface oil and make pores look smaller.

Encyclopedia references list kaolin as an ingredient in facial masks and soaps [1], and describe bentonite as an absorbent clay whose calcium form adsorbs fats and oils [2]. No published clinical trial of clay masks for pore appearance was identified for this article.

paras: Kaolin is a layered clay mineral used as a cosmetic filler and as an ingredient in facial masks and spa treatments [1]. Bentonite is a swelling clay with a large surface area that can adsorb fats, oils and proteins [2]. Bentonite is also a filler, stabilizer and extender in cosmetic and dermatologic formulations [2].

Proponents say that clay pulls sebum from the surface and lets pores look less prominent for a period after use. The physical oil-adsorbing property of bentonite described in reference works is consistent with a surface-oil effect [2], but the references reviewed do not address pore size or appearance on human skin.

Kaolin is described as generally recognized as safe, though it may cause mild skin or mucous-membrane irritation, and some products may contain traces of crystalline silica [1]. Bentonite is described as complying with FDA rules for contact with food and drugs, and a reference in that article notes an FDA consumer warning about one bentonite clay product [2].
